situations.summary: Elmwick folk have twice pulled down Jem Coombe's fence on the Lakemead; Nell Sedge holds the lease and insists the meadow is Reedmoor's to let, while Hob Garrow of Elmwick says it was always Elmwick's common.

sides.Nell Sedge: She let the Lakemead to the Coombes and takes their grain rent; she will not have Elmwick tell her what Reedmoor may let, and she is angry the fence was pulled down.
sides.Jem Coombe: He pays Nell rent in grain and works the meadow; he fears a third fence-pulling and wants Nell to stand behind him.
sides.Morwen Coombe: She keeps the dairy and the strips; she is close with Rowan Wray of Elmwick and hates that the quarrel has come between them.

situations.summary: The Coombes owe Nell Sedge this year's grain rent for the Lakemead, and the harvest is not yet in; Nell has not pressed them but the village tally is short.

sides.Nell Sedge: She keeps the village grain tally and needs the rent to fill the common store; she is fond of the Coombes and has not pressed them yet.
sides.Jem Coombe: He knows the rent is due and the harvest is thin; he is ashamed to ask for time and afraid Nell will take the meadow back.
sides.Morwen Coombe: She counts the dairy and the grain and knows they are short; she would sell cheese to Hilda Sedge's table to make up part of it.

situations.summary: Godric Wade has been courting Wyn Sedge since the spring; both households expect a match, but Nell has not given her word and Godric has no boat of his own yet.

sides.Godric Wade: He wants Wyn and a boat of his own; he fears Nell will not give her son to a fisherman with no boat.
sides.Wyn Sedge: He is fond of Godric and wants the match, but he will not go against his mother's word.
sides.Nell Sedge: She likes Godric well enough but wants to see him with a boat and a net of his own before she gives her word.
sides.Ethelred Wade: He would be glad of the match and has offered Godric a share of his nets, but he cannot give him a boat.

situations.summary: A cough has gone through the reeds and the village's winter store is thinner than it should be; Hilda Sedge and Leofrun Wade are nursing the sick and counting the grain.

sides.Hilda Sedge: She cooks for the common table and tends the cough; she fears the store will not last the winter and has cut the common bake.
sides.Leofrun Wade: She tends the sick with Hilda and knows the barley plots are short; she has sold barley to Brackenford's store against the debt and has little left.
sides.Nell Sedge: She keeps the tally and knows the store is thin; she is weighing whether to buy grain from Thistle Mossfoot's packs or ask Brackenford for time on the debt.

situations.summary: Eadric Sedge owes Thistle Mossfoot for a packet of hooks bought on the east road last season, and the pedlar is due back through Reedmoor with the fibre and salves.

sides.Eadric Sedge: He owes the pedlar for hooks and has not the marks; he would pay in smoked fish if Thistle will take it.
sides.Nell Sedge: She knows her brother's debt and would rather settle it from the common store than have the pedlar go away unpaid.
